bw: Volume of filtrate formed by both kidneys per minute
tp: About 20 percent of cardiac output enters the kidneys to be filtered. GFR is about 125 mL/min in men and 105 mL/min in women.

ww.Renal plasma flow: Renal plasma flow is the plasma entering the kidneys, not the filtrate formed.
ww.Net filtration pressure: NFP is a pressure, not a volume per minute.

evidence: The volume of filtrate formed by both kidneys per minute is termed the glomerular filtration rate (GFR).

bw: Average glomerular filtration rate in men
tp: This is about 180 L/day in men and 150 L/day in women, yet only 1–2 L of urine is produced.

ww.About 12.5 mL/min: This is a tenth of the real value.
ww.About 500 mL/min: This is four times the real value.

evidence: On average, this liter results in the production of about 125 mL/min filtrate produced in men (range of 90 to 140 mL/min) and 105 mL/min filtrate produced in women (range of 80 to 125 mL/min).

bw: Share of the water and solutes filtered by the nephron that is reabsorbed
tp: Reabsorbed substances return to the circulation by the peritubular capillaries and vasa recta.

ww.About 50 percent: Far more than half is reabsorbed.
ww.About 75 percent: The source says 99 percent of the water is reabsorbed.

evidence: All of these substances were “absorbed” in the digestive tract—99 percent of the water and most of the solutes filtered by the nephron must be reabsorbed.

bw: Net filtration pressure in the glomerulus
tp: The low net pressure means small changes in blood osmolarity or capillary pressure cause large changes in filtrate formed.

ww.About 55 mm Hg: 55 mm Hg is only the glomerular hydrostatic pressure.

bw: Created by proteins that stay in the capillary
tp: Bowman’s space has almost no protein, so its osmotic pressure is near zero.

ww.Glomerular blood hydrostatic pressure: This is the force favoring filtration.
ww.Osmotic pressure in Bowman’s space: This is near zero because there are no proteins in the filtrate.

evidence: This means that red and white blood cells, platelets, albumins, and other proteins too large to pass through the filter remain in the capillary, creating an average colloid osmotic pressure of 30 mm Hg within the capillary.

bw: Excess protein leaks into the filtrate
Water moves out of the circulation into tissues
tp: Less osmotic pressure pulls water into the capillaries, so hydrostatic pressure pushes it into the interstitium.

ww.Dehydration: Water is lost from the circulation into tissues rather than from the body.
ww.Hypertension: The described change plumps up tissues; it is not a pressure disorder.

evidence: This “plumps up” the tissues and cells, a condition termed systemic edema.

tp: When pressure drops, the same vessels relax to maintain flow and filtration rate.

ww.It does not respond: Stretching smooth muscle makes it contract, which stabilizes filtration.

evidence: Thus, when blood pressure goes up, smooth muscle in the afferent capillaries contracts to limit any increase in blood flow and filtration rate.

bw: Mean arterial pressure needed to maintain glomerular filtration
tp: MAP is the diastolic pressure plus one-third of the pulse pressure. Pressures below this level cause shock.

ww.About 30 mm Hg: Filtration fails well before MAP falls this low.
ww.About 90 mm Hg: A MAP of 90 is a normal value; the threshold is lower.

evidence: Therefore, if you use mean arterial pressure for the GBHP in the formula for calculating NFP, you can determine that as long as mean arterial pressure is above approximately 60 mm Hg, the pressure will be adequate to maintain glomerular filtration.

bw: Neither reabsorbed nor secreted by the kidney
tp: Inulin clearance is cumbersome clinically, so creatinine is usually used instead.

ww.Glucose: Glucose is almost fully reabsorbed in the PCT.
ww.Urea: About half of urea is reabsorbed and some is secreted.

evidence: Inulin is a plant polysaccharide that is neither reabsorbed nor secreted by the kidney.

tp: Dosing of drugs excreted by the kidney depends on an accurate GFR estimate.

ww.Inulin: Inulin is a plant polysaccharide given intravenously, not a product of muscle metabolism.
ww.Urea: Urea is partly reabsorbed and comes from protein catabolism in the liver.

evidence: However, since measuring inulin clearance is cumbersome in the clinical setting, most often, the GFR is estimated by measuring naturally occurring creatinine, a protein-derived molecule produced by muscle metabolism that is not reabsorbed and only slightly secreted by the nephron.
